concepts.name: SQLite WAL checkpointing
concepts.reason: This is the named research target and the supplied SQLite documentation directly describes its behavior.

concepts.name: Automatic checkpoint configuration
concepts.reason: Thresholds and WAL callbacks determine when automatic checkpoints run.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE
concepts.reason: This mode defines checkpoint progress without waiting for readers or writers.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL
concepts.reason: This mode specifies waiting conditions and completion behavior.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART
concepts.reason: This mode adds reader waiting that enables subsequent WAL reuse.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE
concepts.reason: This mode adds physical WAL truncation to RESTART behavior.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP
concepts.reason: This mode retrieves checkpoint status without checkpointing frames.

concepts.name: Checkpoint lock contention and busy handling
concepts.reason: Lock acquisition and busy-handler outcomes constrain checkpoint execution.

concepts.name: Checkpoint status counters
concepts.reason: The API reports WAL and checkpointed frame counts with explicit exceptional values.

concepts.name: Checkpoint database selection
concepts.reason: Database selection changes operation scope and output validity.

concepts.name: Reader end marks and checkpoint progress
concepts.reason: Reader snapshots constrain how far checkpointing can advance.

concepts.name: Checkpoint starvation
concepts.reason: Overlapping readers can prevent checkpoint completion and permit unbounded WAL growth.

concepts.name: WAL recycling after checkpointing
concepts.reason: WAL reuse has conditions distinct from transferring frames or truncating the file.

concepts.name: Checkpoint synchronization ordering
concepts.reason: Checkpoint correctness depends on storage synchronization before copying and resetting.

concepts.name: Checkpoint scheduling and durability tradeoffs
concepts.reason: Checkpoint placement affects commit latency and interacts with synchronous=NORMAL.

concepts.name: Rollback journaling
concepts.reason: Rollback journaling is a sibling journaling strategy rather than an internal checkpointing concept.

concepts.name: WAL mode activation
concepts.reason: Enabling WAL is configuration context rather than checkpoint execution.

claims.text: A checkpoint moves WAL transactions back into the original database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers automatic checkpointing after a transaction commits if its WAL contains N or more frames.
claims.quote: causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Each new connection defaults to automatic checkpointing with a threshold of 1000 pages or the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT value.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: Passing N less than or equal to zero to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint replaces any existing callback registered through sqlite3_wal_hook().
claims.quote: The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() .

claims.text: Registering a callback through sqlite3_wal_hook() disables automatic checkpointing configured through sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint.
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: Checkpoints initiated by the automatic checkpoint mechanism use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers to finish.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish,

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits using the busy handler until there is no writer and all readers use the most recent database snapshot.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.

claims.text: After its waiting conditions are satisfied, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL checkpoints all log frames and syncs the database file.
claims.quote: It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: While SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL is pending, it blocks new writers but allows new readers to continue unimpeded.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART adds to FULL behavior a post-checkpoint wait, using the busy handler, until all readers read only from the database file.
claims.quote: after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only.

claims.text: Successful completion of SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART ensures that the next writer restarts the WAL from its beginning.
claims.quote: This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE adds to RESTART behavior truncation of the log file to zero bytes immediately before a successful return.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP always checkpoints zero frames.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: If another process already holds the exclusive checkpoint lock for a checkpoint operation, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock on the database file. If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned.

claims.text: Contention for the checkpoint lock does not invoke a configured busy handler.
claims.quote: Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: If the busy handler returns zero while waiting for the writer lock or readers, the checkpoint falls back to PASSIVE behavior and returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: For a non-NULL pnLog, the API reports the total log frame count, or -1 if an error or non-WAL database prevents the checkpoint from running.
claims.quote: *pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file or to -1 if the checkpoint could not run because of an error or because the database is not in WAL mode

claims.text: The pnCkpt count includes frames checkpointed before the current function call.
claims.quote: *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: Successful SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE completion sets both pnLog and pnCkpt output counts to zero.
claims.quote: upon successful completion of an SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE, the log file will have been truncated to zero bytes and so both *pnLog and *pnCkpt will be set to zero.

claims.text: A NULL or empty zDb makes sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 attempt the specified operation on all WAL databases attached to the connection.
claims.quote: If parameter zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db.

claims.text: When zDb selects all attached WAL databases, pnLog and pnCkpt output values are undefined.
claims.quote: In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.

claims.text: Selecting an attached database that is not in WAL mode returns SQLITE_OK and sets both output counters to -1.
claims.quote: If database zDb is the name of an attached database that is not in WAL mode, SQLITE_OK is returned and both *pnLog and *pnCkpt set to -1.

claims.text: A checkpoint must stop when it reaches a WAL page past any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: A checkpoint records its progress in the wal-index and resumes from that position on its next invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: With overlapping readers that always leave at least one reader active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL grows without bound.
claims.quote: if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Attempting checkpoints during reader gaps avoids the overlapping-reader starvation scenario.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: A writer can rewind the WAL when the entire WAL has been transferred and synced and no readers use the WAL.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: Ordinary checkpointing normally recycles the WAL without truncating it, unless journal_size_limit is set.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage before checkpointing moves its content into the database.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database

claims.text: The database file must be synced before the WAL is reset.
claims.quote: and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: By default, the thread performing the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit also runs the automatic checkpoint.
claims.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.text: With PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync operation.
claims.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

claims.text: The described synchronous=NORMAL configuration with separate checkpoint execution can lose committed transactions following a power failure or hard reset.
claims.quote: The downside to this configuration is that transactions are no longer durable and might rollback following a power failure or hard reset.

limitations: Only the frozen source packet was used; no live inventory, retrieval, independent verification, or operational workflow was performed.
S1, S2, and S3 are primary SQLite documentation from one origin, not three independent sources; the standard independent-origin authority floor is unmet.
S2 controls exact checkpoint API semantics where S1's overview differs: S2 documents five modes, and RESTART does not impede readers while pending.
S1's statement that RESTART and TRUNCATE ensure completion must be qualified by S2's busy-handler fallback and SQLITE_BUSY behavior; completion is not unconditional.
Negation checks distinguish checkpointing from truncation, automatic checkpointing from guaranteed completion, and SQLITE_OK from proof that the selected database uses WAL.
The packet does not establish the history or cause of documentation discrepancies, external disagreements, or current behavior beyond these supplied excerpts.
This single bounded extraction does not establish research saturation; the 36-claim cap leaves some supplied API details and operational edge cases unrepresented.
The pass rate is new accepted claims divided by accepted claims in this initial extraction pass; it is not a retrieval-based saturation measurement.
